title: After landslide far-right victory, Germany asks: What just happened?
text:
After landslide far-right victory, Germany asks: What just happened?
Loading...
| Magdeburg, Germany
Germany is taking stock of a dramatically changed political world in the aftermath of a stunning election.
“For many, all that remains is disbelief,” reports Munich’s Süddeutsche Zeitung. “It is an unimaginable moment,” adds the Frankfurter Allgemeine. The country’s leader, Chancellor Friedrich Merz, has said the result has shaken his party “to its very foundations.”
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) won Sunday’s state election in Saxony-Anhalt in a landslide. By taking 43.8% of the vote, the AfD could be the first far-right party to lead a state government since World War II. It is only three seats short of a ruling majority. Negotiations as to who will lead the state are ongoing.
Why We Wrote This
The success of the far-right Alternative for Germany in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt has led to disbelief in a country that has tried to avoid any repetition of its extremist past. Germans are now asking whether the party is a threat to democracy or if, after its electoral success, other parties should work with it.
Two-thirds of Germans say they are concerned about the results, according to a poll by German broadcaster ARD.
Yet this is hardly a result no one saw coming. If anything, recent years have built to this moment with a sense of inevitability. The AfD has been rising, and the German establishment has failed to stop its momentum. Nationally, Politico shows the AfD as the leading party with 28% support.
So Germany is left with questions, many of which feel existential.
Is the AfD a threat to democracy, as the Federal Office for Protection of the Constitution suggests, labeling it extremist? What should the German establishment do now? And how did the AfD get so popular?
Before Sunday, these answers seemed simpler, or at least more distant. Now, for perhaps the first time, Germany is being forced to reconsider all the political assumptions on which its resistance to the AfD has been built.
The new poll already suggests a shift. Despite their concern, 51% of Germans say other parties should work more closely with the AfD. Until now, all other parties have refused to collaborate with the AfD as part of a political “firewall.”
For many Germans, working with the AfD brings echoes of the Weimar government that allowed the Nazis into power in 1933. But how does a democracy exclude a party that wins 43% of the vote – 26 percentage points more than the second-place party?
The way forward is not clear, many agree. But the AfD’s final rally last week before the election in the state capital of Magdeburg offered clues as to why one East German state has essentially mounted a revolt.
“They are all rather boring”
The AfD’s “Family Fest” could be mistaken for a county fair. There are bouncy castles and ice cream stands. Onstage, a musical act sings Bryan Adams’ “Summer of ’69” in a passable American accent. The smell of grilling sausage is snatched away on the breezes of a blustery, late-summer day.
But there is no doubt of the main attraction. A line more than 100 people long unspools out of a tent beside the stage. Here stands Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s candidate for state premier, and one fact immediately becomes glaringly obvious.
This is not your typical German politician.
“Look at our chancellors,” says Markus Ziener, an analyst for the German Marshall Fund of the United States. “They are all rather boring.”
Mr. Siegmund is anything but. He is dashing, with his Nordic-cut stubbled chin and perfectly gelled silver hair. Yet more than that, he gives the appearance of genuinely caring. As the line lengthens, he shows no sign of fatigue. Each visitor gets a handshake or a hug.
During the campaign, he once delivered his message from among a fleet of Simson mopeds, a classic East German brand that evokes plentiful nostalgia. He chronicled behind-the-scenes moments for his TikTok feed, never a hair or a smile out of place.
At a time when Chancellor Merz, a former investment banker with the lowest approval ratings of any chancellor in postwar history (13%), is talking about how to get out of a “climate of gloom and resentment,” Mr. Siegmund is a jolt of political energy.
Mr. Siegmund’s top rival in the election, the state leader of Mr. Merz’s Christian Democratic Union, played by the German playbook, “giving lectures and being very presidential in a way, but this is not working,” says Mr. Ziener.
The CDU finished with 17.2% of the vote, its worst-ever result in the state.
Mr. Siegmund’s approach “is new in the sense that he’s deliberately trying to be approachable, close to the people,” says Mr. Ziener. “All of a sudden, the lady who is the cashier at the supermarket feels heard.”
The scene would have been unthinkable
The AfD began from the ideas of academics pushed to the fringes for their insistence that Germany should stop obsessing about the Holocaust – that it was “a speck of bird poop” in Germany’s long, proud history, as one party leader said.
Mr. Siegmund, a former salesman, is a warning shot to the establishment, not only for his party affiliation, but also for the entire idea of what campaigning is. The AfD now knows that.
“This is what the party is thinking – he is a possible role model for the party,” says Ronald Gläser, an AfD member of the Bundestag, Germany’s federal parliament, from Berlin.
As Mr. Siegmund continues to shake hands and sign T-shirts in Magdeburg, other AfD leaders take the stage. None mince words. Germany is failing because it is being overrun by migrants, one after another says. The only answer, they add, is deportation. The crowd of an estimated 6,000 people roars its approval. T-shirts with nationalist slogans like “Take Back Your Country” or “Volunteer Deportation Assistant” are everywhere.
Even a decade ago, the scene would have been unthinkable.
After the fall of the Nazi regime, West Germany set up politics, law, and education to combat right-wing ideas. The motto ingrained in every schoolchild has been “never again.” Questioning the horrific importance of World War II has never been negotiable. Speaking harshly about migrants has been seen as a potential gateway to the hatred that led to the Holocaust.
But these norms never percolated as deeply in the east. That has given the AfD space to challenge those decades-old taboos.
Gerda Werner does not give an “enemy of the state” vibe at the Family Fest. With her flowing skirt, trendy sunglasses, and vibrant red hair, she is much closer to “cool grandma.” But she’s clear on the problems Germany faces.
“We need to get the serious criminals out,” she says, referring to the migrant community.
“All the other parties only talk and do nothing,” she adds. But looking at the AfD, “I have hope.”
Sebastian Bethke has come to the Family Fest with his family, and while he does not call himself an AfD supporter, he rejects the idea that the party is dangerous. “They are right, but they are not extreme right.” He thinks Die Linke, Germany’s far-left party, is far more extreme.
Is the AfD a threat?
As a lawyer and director of the Max Planck Institute for the Study of Crime, Security, and Law, Ralf Poscher sits at the center of the campaign to protect German democracy.
“It could go both ways,” he says.
On one hand, much of the AfD looks a lot like other European far-right parties. Amid talk about banning the party, Dr. Poscher asks if authorities “really have enough material that [the AfD] wants to abolish democracy in Germany, or do they just have a different program?”
“Asking for more deportations doesn’t pass the bar of being anticonstitutional in a way that a ban would require,” he adds.
Yet there are officials of concern within the AfD, and AfD rallies often draw people with tattoos or clothing linked to Nazi symbology.
“Obviously, there are people in the AfD who fit the bill [for a ban], but it would have to apply to the whole party,” says Dr. Poscher.
For his part, AfD legislator Mr. Gläser says some of these things are beyond the party’s control. He saw three people with a swastika tattoo at a recent rally in Berlin. “We don’t want such people to show up,” he says. “But if you have a rally in Germany, you cannot exclude people by law.”
The political question now is whether other parties should continue excluding the AfD.
Pressure is growing within the CDU to join with the AfD – particularly here in East Germany, where the AfD is strongest. If a few CDU legislators defect in Saxony-Anhalt, it could have sweeping consequences for the party nationally.
To Dr. Poscher, the lesson of recent years is that isolating the AfD has not worked.
“By defending democracy, you will not defend democracy. You need positive politics. If [the establishment] can’t come up with a positive narrative, they will lose. In Germany, that is totally missing.”
Mr. Siegmund is still greeting fans when the blustery day turns into a gale. Gusts snap at tent flaps and push over barriers. Rain comes sideways in sheets that turn layers of clothes into sodden rags. Spectators run for cover, seeking any dry spot amid the storm.
But no one leaves.
Half of Mr. Siegmund’s tent has blown away, but when the wind calms, he is still there, undaunted and undimmed. The emcee hails the crowd, likening it to German iron. When Mr. Siegmund finally takes the stage, spectators emerge from their hiding places like filings drawn to a magnet. Cellphones appear above the crowd, capturing the man and the moment.
Mr. Siegmund speaks of making history, of showing Germany what true democracy is, of sending a message to politics-as-usual in Berlin. Then, he finishes with the phrase that has become his campaign motto – plastered on T-shirts, sung by rappers onstage, and lit on the jumbo screen behind him.
“Everything is possible.”
